attempts.label: DANDI:001261
attempts.paper_title: Comparative Physiology and Morphology of BLA-Projecting NBM/SI Cholinergic Neurons in Mouse and Macaque
attempts.entry_title: BLA-projecting NBM/SI neurons in mouse and macaque (Luo et al. 2024)
attempts.description: Tests the electrophysiological findings of Luo, Jiang, Desai et al. (2024) on dandiset 001261, which holds whole-cell current-clamp recordings of BLA-projecting cholinergic and noncholinergic NBM/SI neurons from 27 mice and 9 macaques. It extracts the paper's electrophysiological features from the current steps and compares cholinergic with noncholinergic mouse neurons and macaque with mouse cholinergic neurons, by rank-sum tests, UMAP and LDA. The morphology of the paper is not in the dandiset.

notebooks.title: Reproducing Luo et al. (2024) from dandiset 001261

outcomes.statement: Electrophysiology was analysed for 48 BLA-projecting cholinergic and 46 BLA-projecting noncholinergic NBM/SI neurons from 27 mice (56 slices) and 46 BLA-projecting cholinergic neurons from nine macaques (38 slices); morphology for 31 mouse cholinergic and 44 mouse noncholinergic neurons.
outcomes.source: Discussion, paragraph 1; Table 1; Results 3.1, paragraph after Figure 1; Results 3.3, paragraph 3
outcomes.quote: In total, we obtained complete analyses of 94 BLA-projecting neurons (48 cholinergic and 46 noncholinergic for electrophysiology; 31 cholinergic and 44 noncholinergic for morphology) from 27 mice (56 slices) and 46 BLA-projecting cholinergic neurons from nine macaques (38 slices)
outcomes.notes: The dandiset has 48 mouse cholinergic, 46 mouse noncholinergic and 46 macaque cholinergic files, from 27 mice and 9 macaques, with the sexes of Table 1 (mice 18 M and 9 F, macaques 7 M and 2 F). One mouse noncholinergic file repeats, sample for sample, a recording also filed as cholinergic (CG608_FL_S4C7_B+G+_-63mV.mat); counted once, the dandiset holds 45 distinct noncholinergic recordings, one fewer than the paper's 46. The four group labels in session_description include none for neurons of unknown ChAT status, so the code's wider reading of the noncholinergic group gives the same count. Four of five counts match. The macaque cholinergic neurons come from 6 of the 9 macaques; read strictly, as 46 cholinergic neurons from nine macaques, the macaque count also fails, and the outcome is partial either way. Slices are not recorded and the morphology is not in the dandiset, so the slice counts and the morphology counts of the statement cannot be checked.
deviations: Each recording deposited twice is counted once (protocol, Author, step 1.2); the mouse recording filed under both groups is counted as cholinergic, as its name says G+ (GFP-positive).

outcomes.statement: In mouse, BLA-projecting cholinergic and noncholinergic NBM/SI neurons differ in 15 of the 18 electrophysiological features; spike width, upstroke and downstroke do not differ.
outcomes.source: Results 3.1, paragraph after the Figure 2 legend; Figure 2D; Figure S2-2C
outcomes.quote: Cholinergic and noncholinergic BLA-projecting neurons within the region of the NBM/SI differed electrophysiologically in all but three features
outcomes.notes: F1 (resting potential) is not in the data, so the count is out of 17 and the criterion's range is 13 to 15. With the adaptation index and the CV on the step with the most spikes (F17 and F18 reading b), 13 of 17 features differ at p < 0.05 under either downstroke reading (48 cholinergic and 45 noncholinergic neurons, NaN values dropped per feature), the lower edge of the range; with the 200 pA step (reading a), 12, below it. Spike width (p = 0.74), upstroke (0.28) and downstroke (0.26) are among the features that do not differ, as the criterion requires, together with AHP latency (0.62). One of the 13, the AHP width, differs in the direction opposite to the paper's (see fig2d-mouse-ahp); counting only differences in the paper's direction would give 12, below the range. The last sweep of a repeated amplitude gives the same counts; the code's variants for input resistance, tau, latency and the AHP give 12 or 13, none against the paper's direction. The resting potential written in 8 cholinergic and 27 noncholinergic file names does not differ (p = 0.36).
deviations: The features are re-implemented in Python (scipy.signal.find_peaks in place of MATLAB findpeaks, scipy curve_fit in place of fit) from the claims file's definitions F1 to F18.

Steps above 200 pA are left out, after Methods 2.4 ("a family of current steps (500 ms duration, -60 to 200 pA amplitude)") and Methods 2.5 (16) ("a current step between 0 and 200 pA"); 23 files also hold steps to 250 pA or more. The steps last 500 or 1000 ms and only their first 500 ms are analysed, as the code does (analysisDuration = 500).

The step onset of each sweep is the first sample of its longest run of non-zero current. Short -20 pA pulses of 50 or 100 ms, alone in a sweep or in the same sweep as a step (0.7 s before it in 8 files, 1.3 s or more after it in the others), are left out as not part of the family of steps (Methods 2.4).

Sag uses the -60 pA step, the closest step below it when there is none, and the next step up when the response is saturated (claims file F2, sagpotential.m). The code's test for saturation cannot fire as written (the mode of the indices of zero differences is at most 1); saturated is read as 1000 or more consecutive identical samples, after the code's comment ("no more than 1000 points will be the same if no saturation"). The -60 pA step whatever its response is shown as a variant.
The rank-sum test is computed as MATLAB ranksum does for these sample sizes (normal approximation with tie and continuity corrections), with scipy's Mann-Whitney U test.
Where an amplitude was recorded more than once, a one-step feature uses the first sweep; the last sweep is shown as a variant and changes no outcome.

The paper's quality control (access resistance, offset current, resting potential) cannot be repeated, as the files do not record these measures; the groups are taken from session_description as deposited.

One macaque cholinergic file (2023_03_06_0002 R+B+A2C1 RMP -78.abf) is left out, as its voltage is 20 times too large; with its voltage divided by 20 it is shown as a variant, which changes no outcome. One copy of each duplicated recording is left out.

outcomes.source: Results 3.1, paragraph after the Figure 2 legend; Figure 2D
outcomes.quote: Overall, noncholinergic neurons were much more excitable than cholinergic ones, with a maximum firing rate almost six times larger (cholinergic 7.3 ± 4.3 Hz, noncholinergic 39.0 ± 24.9 Hz, p < 0.0001)
outcomes.notes: Noncholinergic neurons fire faster, rank-sum p = 1.9e-12 (48 and 45 neurons). The cholinergic mean (6.92 Hz) and both SDs are within tolerance; the noncholinergic mean, 34.8 Hz, is just below its tolerance of 35.1 to 42.9 Hz. The 200 pA reading gives 6.81 and 34.47 Hz.

outcomes.source: Results 3.1, paragraph after the Figure 2 legend; Figure 2D
outcomes.quote: spike threshold: cholinergic -33 ± 4.6 mV, noncholinergic -37.1 ± 6.3 mV, p < 0.001; rheobase current: cholinergic 64.3 ± 41.2 pA, noncholinergic 42.2 ± 33.2 pA, p < 0.001
outcomes.notes: All four means are within tolerance. The threshold test holds (p = 6.5e-4, cholinergic more depolarized). Rheobase is larger in cholinergic neurons but p = 1.1e-3, just above the paper's 0.001 (47 and 44 neurons with a spike). SDs are 4.55 and 6.02 mV (paper 4.6 and 6.3) and 36.3 and 34.1 pA (paper 41.2 and 33.2). The steps of most files are 10 to 50 pA apart, not the 10 pA of the Fig. S2-1 legend, which limits the resolution of the rheobase. One feature of two holds.

outcomes.statement: Mouse cholinergic BLA-projecting neurons have a larger AHP (28.9 +- 8.3 against 12.4 +- 6.1 mV) and a wider AHP (177.9 +- 89.3 against 85.0 +- 118.6 ms) than noncholinergic ones.
outcomes.source: Results 3.1, paragraph after the Figure 2 legend; Figure 2D
outcomes.quote: AHP amplitude: cholinergic 28.9 ± 8.3, noncholinergic 12.4 ± 6.1 mV, p < 0.0001; AHP width: cholinergic 177.9 ± 89.3 ms, noncholinergic 85.0 ± 118.6 ms, p < 0.0001
outcomes.notes: With the Methods' window (rheobase step, minimum within 100 ms of threshold), the AHP amplitude is larger in cholinergic neurons (p = 2.5e-13), the cholinergic mean within tolerance and the noncholinergic mean (16.35 mV) outside it. The AHP width, with its crossings searched within the 100 ms window as the claims file's F14 says, is longer in noncholinergic neurons (298.9 against 183.1 ms, p = 4.1e-5), the opposite of the paper; with the crossings searched to the end of the step it is 226.3 against 160.0 ms (p = 0.017), the same way. The width test does not hold, so the criterion's tests do not both hold and the claim is not reproduced. In 43 of 47 cholinergic and 35 of 43 noncholinergic neurons the potential does not recross the half-amplitude level within the 100 ms window, so the width runs to the end of the analysed 500 ms (latency plus width 495.5 and 495.6 ms on average) and falls with the latency of the first spike (Spearman rho -0.996 and -0.990); these noncholinergic neurons spike earlier (140.9 against 296.3 ms), which gives them the longer widths. In the 4 cholinergic and 8 noncholinergic neurons that recross within the window the width is 9.9 against 54.8 ms (p = 0.051). The code's window (first step with two spikes, afterhyperpolarization.m) gives 30.06 and 12.14 mV and 184.3 and 77.4 ms, all four within tolerance, with p = 4.1e-14 and 5.2e-8; the paper's values match the code's window, not the Methods'. Whether the claims file should judge the AHP on the code's window is asked of a reader (questions/001261.yaml), and which window was used is asked of the paper's authors (finding below). What span F14 should use is also asked of a reader.
deviations: The AHP width with the Methods' window is the time below threshold minus half the AHP amplitude, between the first two crossings within the 100 ms window of F12 (claims file F14, "Window as in F12"), and to the end of the step when the potential does not recross there. The crossings searched to the end of the step are shown as a variant and give the same direction.

The features are re-implemented in Python from the claims file's definitions F1 to F18; steps above 200 pA and short test pulses are left out (Methods 2.4); the step onset is the start of each sweep's longest run of current; duplicated recordings are counted once and the macaque file with a wrong scale is left out.

outcomes.statement: Mouse cholinergic BLA-projecting neurons have a more depolarized resting potential (-54.4 +- 8.4 against -58.7 +- 8.2 mV) and a longer membrane time constant (34.6 +- 14.3 against 22.3 +- 9.8 ms) than noncholinergic ones.
outcomes.source: Results 3.1, paragraph after the Figure 2 legend; Figure 2D
outcomes.quote: Passive electrophysiological properties, such as resting membrane potential (cholinergic -54.4 ± 8.4 mV, noncholinergic -58.7 ± 8.2 mV, p < 0.05) and membrane time constant tau (cholinergic 34.6 ± 14.3, noncholinergic 22.3 ± 9.8 ms, p < 0.0001), also exhibited significant differences
outcomes.notes: The resting potential (F1) is not in the data, as every sweep is recorded with the holding current, so the claim is judged on tau. Tau on the -20 pA step is longer in cholinergic neurons (39.92 against 28.59 ms), but p = 3.2e-3, not below the paper's 0.0001, and both means are above their tolerance (31.14 to 38.06 and 20.07 to 24.53 ms), so tau does not hold. The code's step (the most negative unsaturated step from -50 to 0 pA) gives 34.88 against 22.04 ms, both within tolerance, p = 2.7e-6, a variant that does not decide. The -20 pA fits explain a median 84% (cholinergic) and 91% (noncholinergic) of the variance of the trace, and 33 cholinergic and 21 noncholinergic fits explain less than 90%. Keeping only the fits with R^2 of 0.9 or more (14 and 24 neurons), tau is 47.02 against 33.97 ms, p = 5.1e-3, which does not hold either. The outcome follows the criterion, but it may reflect noisy fits on a small step more than the neurons. The first two measured values are the resting potentials written in 8 cholinergic and 27 noncholinergic file names, a subset that does not decide; they are close to the paper's -54.4 and -58.7 mV but do not differ (p = 0.36).

outcomes.statement: In mouse, spike amplitude, the CV of interspike intervals and sag also differ between cholinergic and noncholinergic BLA-projecting neurons, with cholinergic neurons having larger spikes, a lower CV and a smaller sag.
outcomes.source: Figure S2-2A
outcomes.quote: Additional electrophysiological features that distinguish BLA-projecting, cholinergic from noncholinergic neurons and features that are shared in mouse NBM/SI
outcomes.notes: Spike amplitude is larger in cholinergic neurons (59.65 against 53.35 mV, p = 5.4e-5, within p <= 0.001). The CV of the intervals is lower in cholinergic neurons on the step with the most spikes (0.190 against 0.317, p = 1.3e-3, within p <= 0.01); on the 200 pA step p = 0.011. Sag is smaller in cholinergic neurons (1.86 against 3.19 mV, p = 1.8e-3, within p <= 0.01). The sag rests on the claims file's rule for a saturated -60 pA response, which applies to two cholinergic and five noncholinergic mouse neurons whose -60 pA response is clipped at -100 or -105.5 mV for 1144 to 4793 samples. On the -60 pA step whatever its response the sag is 1.80 against 3.01 mV, p = 0.011, which misses the figure's 0.01, so the outcome rests on the reading of saturation (assumption below). Question for the paper's authors (finding below).
deviations: Assumed, as the code's test for a saturated response cannot fire as written (sagpotential.m, the mode of the indices of zero differences is at most 1), that a saturated response is one with 1000 or more consecutive identical samples, after the code's comment ("no more than 1000 points will be the same if no saturation"). The 7 mouse responses it catches are clipped at -100 or -105.5 mV for 1144 to 4793 samples. Without the rule sag gives p = 0.011, so the outcome rests on this reading.

The features are re-implemented in Python from the claims file's definitions F1 to F18; steps above 200 pA and short test pulses are left out (Methods 2.4); the step onset is the start of each sweep's longest run of current; duplicated recordings are counted once and the macaque file with a wrong scale is left out; the rank-sum test has MATLAB's tie and continuity corrections.

outcomes.statement: A UMAP of the 18 electrophysiological features separates mouse cholinergic from noncholinergic BLA-projecting neurons almost completely, with only two neurons on the wrong side of the boundary.
outcomes.source: Results 3.1, last paragraph; Figure 2C
outcomes.quote: shows almost complete separation between the BLA-projecting cholinergic and noncholinergic neurons within the NBM/SI; only two neurons fall on the "wrong" side of the boundary
outcomes.notes: On 17 features (F1 not computable), the UMAP separates the groups better than every one of 1000 label permutations for all 10 seeds under both readings of missing values, but a linear boundary in the UMAP plane misclassifies a median of 4 neurons (range 4 to 6, 85 neurons with every feature, 14 components) or 8.5 (8 to 10, 93 neurons with missing values imputed, 15 components), not 2. It fails under both readings. With n_neighbors 5 or 30, or min_dist 0.1 or 0.5, the median is 4 to 7 (dropped) and 8 to 10.5 (imputed).
deviations: UMAP is umap-learn 0.5 with n_neighbors 15 and min_dist 0.3, the defaults of Meehan's run_umap the paper used, in place of the MATLAB implementation; the claims file calls the package defaults a standard choice. Other values of both parameters are shown and change no outcome.
The features are re-implemented in Python from the claims file's definitions; F1 is left out of the 18, as it is not in the data.

outcomes.statement: Mouse cholinergic and noncholinergic BLA-projecting neurons differ in 3 of 13 morphological features; cholinergic neurons have more branch points (8.1 +- 5.4 against 6.6 +- 5.4), a smaller total process area (4.6 +- 2.7 against 6.6 +- 3.6 x 10^3 um^2) and a smaller centripetal bias (12.9 +- 14.9 against 15.2 +- 10.1).
outcomes.source: Results 3.2, paragraph after the Figure 4 legend; Figure 4D; Figure S4-1B
outcomes.quote: Three of the 13 features assayed were statistically significantly different ... cholinergic neurons had more branch points (cholinergic 8.1 ± 5.4, noncholinergic 6.6 ± 5.4, p < 0.05), a smaller total proximal process area ... and a smaller centripetal bias (cholinergic 12.9 ± 14.9, noncholinergic 15.2 ± 10.1, p < 0.05)
outcomes.notes: The morphological features are not in the dandiset, which holds only current-clamp recordings (its asset summary lists CurrentClampSeries and CurrentClampStimulusSeries), and the paper's Data Availability Statement names only the DANDI Archive. No other public copy was found.

outcomes.statement: Sholl intersections as a function of distance from the soma do not differ between mouse cholinergic and noncholinergic BLA-projecting neurons.
outcomes.source: Results 3.2, paragraph after the Figure 4 legend; Figure S4-1A
outcomes.quote: On a standard Sholl analysis of intersections as a function of distance from the soma, cholinergic and noncholinergic neurons were also not significantly different
outcomes.notes: The Sholl counts are not in the dandiset, nor public elsewhere as far as the paper says (Data Availability Statement names only the DANDI Archive).

outcomes.statement: A UMAP of the morphological features does not separate mouse cholinergic from noncholinergic BLA-projecting neurons.
outcomes.source: Results 3.2, paragraph after the Figure 4 legend; Figure 4C
outcomes.quote: Dimensionality reduction via PCA and subsequent display via UMAP likewise indicated that proximal neuritic morphology was similar between the two types of mouse BLA-projecting neurons
outcomes.notes: Needs the 13 morphological features, which are not in the dandiset nor public elsewhere.

outcomes.statement: A linear discriminant analysis of the electrophysiological features clearly separates mouse cholinergic from noncholinergic BLA-projecting neurons.
outcomes.source: Results 3.2, paragraph before the Figure 5 legend; Figure 5A
outcomes.quote: Given the clean separation between these groups on the unsupervised electrophysiological UMAP plot ... supervised LDA revealed a clear separation
outcomes.notes: The LDA classifies 98.8% of the 85 neurons with every feature and 94.6% of all 93 with missing values imputed, for both scalings, above the 95th percentile (0.74 to 0.76) and the maximum (0.81 to 0.84) of 1000 shuffles of either kind (p = 0.001 in each case). The 10-fold cross-validated accuracy, with the imputation and scaling fitted on the training folds only, is 0.89 to 0.95.
deviations: LDA is scikit-learn's LinearDiscriminantAnalysis (pooled covariance) in place of MATLAB fitcdiscr, on 17 features (F1 is not in the data).

outcomes.statement: AHP amplitude has the highest weight in the LDA separating mouse cholinergic from noncholinergic BLA-projecting neurons.
outcomes.source: Results 3.2, paragraph before the Figure 5 legend; Figure 5B
outcomes.quote: The feature with the highest weight in the LDA vector was AHP amplitude
outcomes.notes: AHP amplitude has the largest weight under both readings of the weights and both readings of missing values (absolute coefficient 9.50 and 6.62, next 7.49 and 1.91; coefficient times mean difference 14.28 and 9.79, next 9.22 and 2.49).
deviations: LDA is scikit-learn's in place of MATLAB fitcdiscr, on 17 z-scored features (F1 is not in the data).

outcomes.statement: An LDA of the morphological features fails to separate mouse cholinergic from noncholinergic BLA-projecting neurons; the result is like that of shuffled features.
outcomes.source: Results 3.2, paragraph before the Figure 5 legend; Figure 5C
outcomes.quote: By contrast, even supervised LDA failed to separate cholinergic and noncholinergic neurons morphologically ... Indeed, the distribution was equivalent to the LDA plots that resulted when feature values were randomly shuffled
outcomes.notes: Needs the 13 morphological features, which are not in the dandiset nor public elsewhere.

outcomes.statement: Macaque BLA-projecting cholinergic neurons are more excitable than mouse ones, with a maximum firing rate three times larger (26.3 +- 23.1 against 7.3 +- 4.3 Hz), a rheobase a third as large (23.3 +- 16.5 against 64.3 +- 41.2 pA) and an f-I slope twice as large (0.13 +- 0.10 against 0.06 +- 0.03 Hz/pA).
outcomes.source: Results 3.3, paragraph after the Figure 7 legend; Figure 7D
outcomes.quote: The maximum firing rate was three times larger (macaque 26.3 ± 23.1 Hz, mouse 7.3 ± 4.3 Hz, p < 0.0001), the rheobase current was only a third as large (macaque 23.3 ± 16.5 pA, mouse 64.3 ± 41.2 pA, p < 0.0001), and the slope of the f - I curve was twice as large (macaque 0.13 ± 0.10, mouse 0.06 ± 0.03, p < 0.0001)
outcomes.notes: All three tests hold in the reported direction at p < 0.0001 (maximum rate p = 7.2e-12, rheobase 6.1e-11, f-I slope 9.3e-6; 45 macaque and 48 mouse neurons, 45 and 47 with a spike). The rheobase and both f-I slopes are within tolerance; the macaque maximum rate, 21.47 Hz, is below the tolerance of 23.67 to 28.93 Hz. The code's maximum over every step, including the steps above 200 pA that some macaque files hold, gives 24.04 Hz, and with the rescaled macaque file added the maximum rate is 22.3 Hz; these variants do not decide.
deviations: The features are re-implemented in Python (scipy.signal.find_peaks in place of MATLAB findpeaks, scipy curve_fit in place of fit) from the claims file's definitions F1 to F18.

Steps above 200 pA are left out, after Methods 2.4 ("a family of current steps (500 ms duration, -60 to 200 pA amplitude)") and Methods 2.5 (16) ("a current step between 0 and 200 pA"); 23 files also hold steps to 250 pA or more. The steps last 500 or 1000 ms and only their first 500 ms are analysed, as the code does (analysisDuration = 500).

The step onset of each sweep is the first sample of its longest run of non-zero current. Short -20 pA pulses of 50 or 100 ms, alone in a sweep or in the same sweep as a step (0.7 s before it in 8 files, 1.3 s or more after it in the others), are left out as not part of the family of steps (Methods 2.4).

Sag uses the -60 pA step, the closest step below it when there is none, and the next step up when the response is saturated (claims file F2, sagpotential.m). The code's test for saturation cannot fire as written (the mode of the indices of zero differences is at most 1); saturated is read as 1000 or more consecutive identical samples, after the code's comment ("no more than 1000 points will be the same if no saturation"). The -60 pA step whatever its response is shown as a variant.
The rank-sum test is computed as MATLAB ranksum does for these sample sizes (normal approximation with tie and continuity corrections), with scipy's Mann-Whitney U test.
Where an amplitude was recorded more than once, a one-step feature uses the first sweep; the last sweep is shown as a variant and changes no outcome.

outcomes.statement: Macaque BLA-projecting cholinergic neurons have a more hyperpolarized spike threshold (-39.7 +- 5.9 against -33.0 +- 4.6 mV), a smaller AHP (19.1 +- 8.8 against 28.9 +- 8.3 mV) and a narrower AHP (106.6 +- 71.9 against 177.9 +- 89.3 ms) than mouse ones.
outcomes.source: Results 3.3, paragraph after the Figure 7 legend; Figure 7D
outcomes.quote: spike threshold: macaque -39.7 ± 5.9 mV, mouse -33.0 ± 4.6 mV, p < 0.0001) and in afterhyperpolarization properties (AHP amplitude: macaque 19.1 ± 8.8 mV, mouse 28.9 ± 8.3 mV, p < 0.0001; AHP width: macaque 106.6 ± 71.9 ms, mouse 177.9 ± 89.3 ms, p < 0.0001)
outcomes.notes: Two of three tests hold. The macaque threshold is more hyperpolarized (-39.42 against -33.12 mV, p = 2.4e-7) and the AHP smaller (20.76 against 31.26 mV, p = 6.8e-9), both macaque means within tolerance. With the Methods' window the AHP width does not differ (224.4 against 183.1 ms, p = 0.17; 187.0 against 160.0 ms, p = 0.32, with the crossings searched to the end of the step). The code's window gives 119.1 against 184.3 ms (p = 3.5e-4), the macaque narrower as in the paper, its mean just above the tolerance of 95.9 to 117.3 ms. With the Methods' window the potential does not recross within 100 ms in 36 of 45 macaque and 43 of 47 mouse neurons, so the width mostly measures the time from the first spike to the end of the step. The window is asked of a reader (questions/001261.yaml).
deviations: The AHP width with the Methods' window is measured as for fig2d-mouse-ahp; both readings of its window are shown and give the same outcome.

outcomes.quote: In all, 15 of the 18 electrophysiological features were insignificantly different between macaque and mouse

outcomes.statement: A UMAP of the 18 electrophysiological features shows a strong separation between macaque and mouse BLA-projecting cholinergic neurons.
outcomes.source: Results 3.3, last paragraph; Figure 7C; Discussion 4.3, paragraph 1
outcomes.quote: The resulting 2D UMAP plot is given in Figure 7C . It exhibits a strong separation between groups
outcomes.notes: The criterion's reading (b) holds and reading (a) fails, the case it makes methods_underspecified. The separation beats every one of 1000 label permutations for all 10 seeds under both readings of missing values, but a linear boundary misclassifies a median of 9 (range 9 to 10, of 88 neurons) and 9 (8 to 10, of 93), not at most 2. With n_neighbors 5 or 30, or min_dist 0.1 or 0.5, the median is 8.5 to 10.5. The paper does not say how it judged a separation strong. Question for the paper's authors (finding below).

outcomes.statement: Macaque BLA-projecting cholinergic neurons have a larger convex hull than mouse ones, in volume (2.19 +- 1.63 against 0.94 +- 0.77, units below), area (1.15 +- 0.59 against 0.83 +- 0.45 x 10^5 um^2) and sphericity (0.65 +- 0.08 against 0.51 +- 0.09).
outcomes.source: Results 3.4, paragraph after the Figure 8 legend; Figure 9D
outcomes.quote: Most notably, those related to convex hull were different (convex hull volume: macaque 2.19 ± 1.63 × 10 3 ... convex hull sphericity: macaque 0.65 ± 0.08, mouse 0.51 ± 0.09, p < 0.0001)
outcomes.notes: The convex hull features are not in the dandiset nor public elsewhere.

outcomes.statement: Of the 13 morphological features, five (text) or six (Figure 9 legend) differ between macaque and mouse BLA-projecting cholinergic neurons; the other seven are similar.
outcomes.source: Results 3.4, paragraph after the Figure 8 legend; Figure 9 legend; Figure S9-1B
outcomes.quote: five of the 13 measured parameters exhibited significant differences
outcomes.notes: The morphological features are not in the dandiset nor public elsewhere.

outcomes.statement: The proximal arbors of macaque BLA-projecting cholinergic neurons tend to have fewer branch points than those of mouse.
outcomes.source: Discussion, paragraph 2; Figure 9D
outcomes.quote: the soma-proximal arbors of macaque BLA-projecting NBM/SI cholinergic neurons tend to have fewer branch points and occupy larger 3D space than those of mouse
outcomes.notes: The branch point counts are not in the dandiset nor public elsewhere.

outcomes.statement: In a UMAP of the morphological features, macaque neurons tend to cluster away from mouse neurons, but the separation is weak compared with the electrophysiological UMAP.
outcomes.source: Results 3.4, paragraph before Figure 10; Figure 9C
outcomes.quote: There was a tendency for macaque neurons to cluster away from mouse neurons ... but the effect of clustering based on morphology alone was weak
outcomes.notes: Needs the morphological features, which are not in the dandiset nor public elsewhere; it also depends on fig7c-macaque-mouse-umap-separation, which is blocked as methods_underspecified.

outcomes.statement: Combining the 18 electrophysiological and 13 morphological features separates macaque from mouse BLA-projecting cholinergic neurons, in a UMAP and clearly in an LDA, unlike shuffled data.
outcomes.source: Results 3.4, paragraph before Figure 10; Figure 10A and B
outcomes.quote: Examination of combined morphoelectric features distinguishes macaque versus mouse basal forebrain neurons despite common projection target, anatomical location, and cholinergic phenotype ... Note the clear separation in clustering of the two populations from one another and its distinct nature from the distribution of shuffled data
outcomes.notes: Needs the morphological features of the 46 macaque and 27 mouse cholinergic neurons, which are not in the dandiset nor public elsewhere.

outcomes.statement: The features with the highest LDA weights separating macaque from mouse are convex hull (morphology) and rheobase, AHP width and maximum firing rate (physiology).
outcomes.source: Results 3.4, paragraph before Figure 10; Figure 10C
outcomes.quote: The features with the highest weight in the LDA vector analysis differentiating macaque from mouse were convex hull in morphology and rheobase, AHP width, and maximum firing rate in physiology
outcomes.notes: Depends on fig10-combined-separation, blocked for lack of the morphological features.

outcomes.statement: Sholl intersections as a function of distance from the soma are similar in macaque and mouse BLA-projecting cholinergic neurons.
outcomes.source: Results 3.4, paragraph after the Figure 8 legend; Figure S9-1A
outcomes.quote: Although many morphological features were similar
outcomes.notes: The Sholl counts are not in the dandiset nor public elsewhere.

findings.statement: The recording CG608_FL_S4C7_B+G+_-63mV.mat is deposited twice with identical traces, once as a mouse cholinergic neuron (sub-CG608 obj-1ukhfn8) and once as a mouse noncholinergic neuron (sub-CG608 obj-17liqyi). Its name says G+ (GFP-positive, cholinergic). Counted once, the dandiset holds 45 distinct mouse noncholinergic recordings, not the paper's 46.

The macaque noncholinergic recording NHP_20220420-03 of M#12 Shahruk is deposited twice with identical traces, under two session names (one of them with spaces in place of hyphens). Counted once, the dandiset holds 11 macaque noncholinergic neurons, as the paper says.

In the macaque file "2023_03_06_0002 R+B+A2C1 RMP -78.abf" (sub-M#19-29511 obj-1nl2qam) the voltage is 20 times too large (baseline -1557 "mV"; divided by 20 it is -77.9 mV, the value in its name), while its conversion factor is 1.
The stimulus series are labelled amperes but hold pA (values -100 to 1200).

The amplifier fields of every sweep of every file hold one value each (bias current 1e-11 A, bridge balance 2e7 Ohm, capacitance compensation 1e-12 F, gain 1), although the neurons were held at -65 mV by a bias current set per neuron (Methods 2.4); they are placeholders.

Most sweeps hold a short -20 pA test pulse besides the step, and nothing in the files marks which part of the stimulus is the step. In 8 files (six mouse cholinergic neurons of November 2021 to February 2022 and two macaque neurons of M#11) the pulse starts 0.7 s before the step in every sweep that holds a step; in the others it starts 1.3 s or more after the step onset. An analysis that takes the first non-zero stimulus sample as the step onset misses the step in those 8 files.

The -60 pA responses of 8 neurons (seven mouse, one macaque) are clipped at -100 or -105.5 mV for 1144 to 4793 samples, the limit of the recording; their sag is measured on the next step up, as the paper's code intends.

The resting potential (feature 1 of Methods 2.5, "measured in the absence of a current injection") is not recorded; every sweep carries the holding current. Some original file names, kept as the NWB identifier, carry a value (63 of 152 files).

The morphology of the paper (13 features, Sholl counts, reconstructions of 31 and 44 mouse and 52 macaque neurons) is not in the dandiset, whose description says it holds the physiology data, and the paper names no other archive.

The files record neither the quality-control measures (access resistance, offset current) nor the slice of each neuron; general/notes holds only a bregma position. The original file names carry labels such as R+, B+, G+ and B+R- that are not documented and do not follow session_description consistently (a macaque file named R+B+G+ is filed as noncholinergic, and of three named B+R- two are filed as cholinergic and one as noncholinergic).
Two files in the folder of mouse CG608 (subject_id CG608) are named for mouse CG609 (CG609_FL_S7LC4_B+G+_-62mV.mat, CG609_FL_S6RC1_B+G+_-67mV.mat).

The current steps differ between files and from the paper's description. The increments up to 200 pA are 10 to 50 pA in most files, include 5 pA in 24 files and are 100 pA in one, not the 10 pA of the Fig. S2-1 legend; 23 files go above 200 pA (one to 1200 pA); the steps last 500 or 1000 ms, not 500 ms.
The 46 macaque cholinergic files come from 6 of the 9 macaques, while the paper reports 46 cholinergic neurons from nine macaques.

The paper's code (afterhyperpolarization.m, commit 17a3265) measures the AHP on the first step with two spikes, between 0.75 ms before the first and the second peak, while Methods 2.5 (12 to 14) measure it after the first spike within 100 ms. On this dandiset the code's window gives all four mouse AHP means of the Results within 10% (30.1 and 12.1 mV, 184.3 and 77.4 ms against 28.9, 12.4, 177.9 and 85.0) and the Methods' window does not (noncholinergic AHP width 298.9 ms, longer than the cholinergic 183.1 ms).

The paper's code (inputresistance.m, commit 17a3265) fits the membrane time constant on the most negative unsaturated step between -50 and 0 pA, while Methods 2.5 (4) use the -20 pA step. On this dandiset the code's step gives the paper's mouse values (34.9 and 22.0 ms against 34.6 and 22.3) and the -20 pA step does not (39.9 and 28.6 ms).

Question for the paper's authors. Which window produced the AHP amplitude, latency and width reported in Results 3.1 and 3.3, the Methods' (rheobase step, 100 ms after threshold) or the code's (first step with two spikes)? And for the Methods' window, over what span is the AHP width at half maximum measured?

Question for the paper's authors. How is a saturated -60 pA response recognised for the sag? The test in sagpotential.m (the mode of the indices of zero differences above 1000) cannot be met as written; this attempt reads it as 1000 or more consecutive identical samples, which moves the sag of 7 mouse neurons to the next step up and decides whether the mouse sag difference reaches p < 0.01.

Question for the paper's authors. Methods 2.5 (17, 18) measure the adaptation index and the CV "for the maximal current step"; is that the 200 pA step or the step with the most spikes, as in spikefrequencyadaptation.m? The mouse adaptation difference holds only with the latter.

Question for the paper's authors. How was the separation of the UMAP plots judged (the "wrong side of the boundary" of Fig. 2C and the "strong separation" of Fig. 7C)? A linear boundary in the UMAP plane misclassifies 4 to 10 neurons here in either comparison.
Question for the paper's authors. Where was the resting potential (feature 1) recorded, and for how many neurons? The deposited sweeps all carry the holding current.

disagreements.reason: AHP amplitude has p = 3.7e-12, but the NC mean is 16.35 against 12.4 +- 1.24. AHP width under the Methods window is reversed, C 158.9, NC 226.3, p = 0.02 (the window-only reading is also reversed, p = 2.6e-5). The tests do not hold, so this is not even partial. The code's window does reproduce it, 29.7 / 12.1 mV and 180.8 / 77.4 ms (cell 27). The claims file making the Methods window the deciding reading is a likely misreading of what the paper computed (problem 2), and the main F14 searches to the end of the step where the claims file says "Window as in F12" (problem 3).

F1 can't be computed (file names give it for only 8 of 48 C neurons, p = 0.35). Tau has p = 6.7e-5 in the right direction, but the means are far outside tolerance, C 60.95 against 34.6 +- 3.46, NC 28.6 against 22.3 +- 2.23 (cell 31). The mouse C tau values are very large (CG250 401 ms, CG269 153 ms), which the onset error may explain; a plot or a fit-quality metric for the tau outliers would show whether these are failed fits or bad windows.
Means match (1.32 and 1.18), but p = 0.025 does not reach the criterion's p < 0.01 (cell 45).

entries.title: BLA-projecting NBM/SI neurons in mouse and macaque (Luo et al. 2024)
entries.description: Tests the electrophysiological findings of Luo, Jiang, Desai et al. (2024) on dandiset 001261, which holds whole-cell current-clamp recordings of BLA-projecting cholinergic and noncholinergic NBM/SI neurons from 27 mice and 9 macaques. It extracts the paper's electrophysiological features from the current steps and compares cholinergic with noncholinergic mouse neurons and macaque with mouse cholinergic neurons, by rank-sum tests, UMAP and LDA. The morphology of the paper is not in the dandiset.
